newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian PM sends envoy to troubled PNG.
newsitem.headline: Australian PM sends envoy to troubled PNG.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard said on Wednesday he would send his chief diplomat to Papua New Guinea to help resolve the crisis over Port Moresby's hiring of mercenaries to quell an island rebellion.
In a special statement to parliament, Howard said Papua New Guinea Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan had welcomed the move.
Australian officials said Foreign Affairs Department chief Philip Flood would fly to the troubled South Pacific nation aboard an airforce VIP jet on Wednesday night.

Howard said he had spoken to Chan by telephone on Wednesday, backing the Papua New Guinea leader's decision to sack rebellious military chief Jerry Singirok, but reaffirming Australia's bitter opposition to the mercenary plan.
"I reiterated ... the continuing opposition of the Australian government to the deployment of mercenaries on Bougainville," Howard said.
"I will be sending a personal emissary to Port Moresby as soon as possible to continue on my behalf..."

Flood will be joined by defence intelligence chief Hugh White and another senior diplomat, former High Commissioner to Papua New Guinea Allan Taylor. The mission will discuss alternatives to the mercenary strategy.
Chan's use of mercenaries had sparked a political crisis in his country and threatened Port Moresby's relations with neighbouring governments.

It has also led to calls for Australia to cut its A$320 million (US$253 million) aid to Port Moresby, although Foreign Minister Alexander Downer said earlier on Wednesday that such a move would be counter-productive.

Australia and New Zealand have both backed Chan over his decision to sack Singirok, who had demanded Chan quit over his plan to hire mercenaries to quell a secessionist rebellion on Bougainville island.

Chan last month agreed a A$36 million contract with a British-based mercenary company to train his under-equipped and poorly-trained troops -- but the cost of the deal has enraged both officers and rank-and-file troops.
Howard told parliament that there was "reasonable alternatives" to what he termed "the sordid use of mercenaries in our part of the world".
He did not provide details, but Australian media have speculated that Canberra could boost its training of Papua New Guinea soldiers if Chan cancels the mercenary contract.
